questions.question: Growing wheat and mustard simultaneously on the same piece of land is an example of which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mixed cropping**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mixed cropping** is an agricultural practice where **two or more crops** are grown simultaneously on the **same piece of land**.
 
• This method is primarily used as a **risk management** strategy to ensure that even if one crop fails due to **adverse weather conditions**, pests, or diseases, the farmer can still harvest the other crop.
 
• Common combinations in India include **Wheat + Mustard**, **Wheat + Gram**, or **Groundnut + Sunflower**. In these cases, seeds are typically mixed before sowing, and there is no **definite row pattern**.
 
• **Crop rotation** is the practice of growing a **series of different types of crops** in the same area in **sequential seasons**. It is done to maintain **soil fertility** and break pest cycles, but since the crops are not grown simultaneously, ***statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Jhum cultivation**, also known as **shifting cultivation** or **slash and burn** agriculture, involves clearing a patch of **forest land**, burning the vegetation, and farming it for a few years before moving to a new plot. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Mixed cropping** directly describes the simultaneous growth of wheat and mustard on one plot. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Monoculture cropping** refers to the agricultural practice of growing only a **single crop** (such as corn, wheat, or rice) year after year on the same land. It lacks the **biodiversity** seen in mixed cropping. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Intercropping:**
 
 
• While similar to mixed cropping, **intercropping** involves growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same field in a **definite row pattern** (e.g., a **1:1** or **1:2 ratio**).
 
• It aims for better **utilization of resources** like sunlight, water, and nutrients, as the crops selected usually have different **nutrient requirements** or **canopy heights**.
 
 
 
• **Shifting Cultivation (Jhum):**
 
 
• This is widely practiced in the **hilly regions** of **Northeast India** (like **Assam, Nagaland, and Manipur**).
 
• While it provides subsistence, it is often associated with **soil erosion** and **loss of forest cover** when the fallow periods are shortened.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Mixed Cropping:**
 
 
• It increases the **yield per unit area** and provides **diversity in food supply** for the farmer's family.
 
• Different crops have different **root depths**, which helps in efficient **nutrient uptake** from different layers of the soil.
 
• Leguminous crops (like gram) are often paired with cereals (like wheat) because they help in **nitrogen fixation**, improving **soil health** naturally.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Wheat (Triticum aestivum):** It is a major **Rabi crop** in India, typically sown in **October-November** and harvested in **March-April**. It requires a **cool growing season** and bright sunshine at the time of ripening.
 
• **Mustard (Brassica):** It is an **oilseed crop** also grown during the **Rabi season**. It is often used in mixed cropping with wheat because both crops have similar **climatic requirements** but differ in their **morphology**.
 
• **Sustainable Agriculture:** Mixed cropping and crop rotation are considered key components of **sustainable farming** as they reduce the dependency on **chemical fertilizers** and synthetic **pesticides**.
</ul

questions.question:
**Match the following synthetic indicators and colour changes.** 
 **Column A (Indicator)** <span style="font-size
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Red Litmus**: This is a **natural indicator** used to detect the presence of **bases**. In an **acidic solution**, it remains **red**, but it **turns blue** when introduced to a **basic (alkaline) solution**. ***Hence, A matches with 1 is correct.***
 
• **Blue Litmus**: This indicator is used to test for **acidity**. In a **basic solution**, it remains **blue**, but it **turns red** when it comes into contact with an **acidic solution**. ***Hence, B matches with 2 is correct.***
 
• **Phenolphthalein**: This is a well-known **synthetic indicator** often used in **acid-base titrations**. It is **colourless in acidic** or neutral environments and **turns pink** (or deep fuchsia) in **basic solutions** where the **pH** is above **8.2**. ***Hence, C matches with 3 is correct.***
 
• **Methyl Orange**: Another common **synthetic indicator**, it exhibits a clear color change based on the **pH level**. It **turns red in acidic** solutions (pH below 3.1) and **turns yellow in basic** or neutral solutions (pH above 4.4). ***Hence, D matches with 4 is correct.***
 
• Indicators are essential tools in **chemistry** to determine the **chemical nature** of a substance without needing complex machinery. ***Hence, the correct match is A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Indicators**: Indicators are generally classified into three types: **Natural**, **Synthetic**, and **Olfactory**.
 
 
• **Natural Indicators**: These are derived from plants. Examples include **Litmus** (from **Lichens**), **Turmeric**, and **Red Cabbage** juice.
 
• **Synthetic Indicators**: These are prepared in laboratories. Examples include **Phenolphthalein** and **Methyl Orange**.
 
• **Olfactory Indicators**: These change their **smell/odor** in acidic or basic media. Common examples are **onion**, **clove oil**, and **vanilla essence**.
 
 
 
• **The pH Scale**: Developed by **S.P.L. Sorensen** in **1909**, the **pH scale** measures the **hydrogen ion concentration**. It ranges from **0 to 14**, where **7 is neutral**, less than 7 is **acidic**, and more than 7 is **basic**.
 
• **Universal Indicator**: This is a mixture of several different indicators that shows **different colours** at different **concentrations of hydrogen ions** in a solution, allowing for a more precise determination of **pH**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Litmus Extraction**: **Litmus solution** is a purple dye extracted from **Lichens**, which belong to the division **Thallophyta**. It is the most commonly used **acid-base indicator** in laboratories worldwide.
 
• **Turmeric as an Indicator**: **Turmeric** remains **yellow** in the presence of **acids** but turns **reddish-brown** in the presence of a **base**. This is why a curry stain on a white shirt turns red when washed with **soap** (which is basic).
 
• **Reaction in Neutral Solutions**: Indicators like **Methyl Orange** and **Phenolphthalein** have specific **transition ranges**. For instance, distilled water (neutral) will not change the colour of phenolphthalein, keeping it **colourless**.
 
• **Application**: These indicators are vital in industries such as **wastewater treatment**, **agriculture** (soil testing), and **medicine** to monitor and control **chemical reactions**.
</ul

questions.question: Which method is used to extract metals that are high in the reactivity series?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Electrolytic reduction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Metals located at the top of the **reactivity series**, such as **Potassium (K)**, **Sodium (Na)**, **Calcium (Ca)**, **Magnesium (Mg)**, and **Aluminium (Al)**, are highly reactive and are never found in nature as free elements.
 
• These metals cannot be extracted from their compounds by **heating with carbon**. This is because these highly reactive metals have a much higher affinity for **oxygen** than **carbon** does, meaning carbon cannot act as a **reducing agent** for their oxides.
 
• The method used for the extraction of these high-reactivity metals is **Electrolytic reduction**. This process involves passing an **electric current** through the molten state of their ionic compounds (usually chlorides or oxides).
 
• During **electrolysis**, the metal ions (which are **positively charged**) are attracted to and deposited at the **Cathode** (the **negatively charged electrode**). For example, **Sodium** is obtained by the electrolysis of **molten Sodium Chloride (NaCl)**.
 
• In the case of **Aluminium**, it is extracted from its ore through the **Hall-Héroult process**, which involves the **electrolytic reduction** of molten **Alumina (Al2O3)**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Electrolytic reduction.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Roasting**:
 
 
• This process is primarily used for **sulfide ores**. It involves heating the ore strongly in the presence of **excess air** or **oxygen**.
 
• The goal is to convert sulfide ores into **metal oxides**, which are easier to reduce. For instance, **Zinc sulfide (ZnS)** is roasted to produce **Zinc oxide (ZnO)**.
 
 
 
• **Calcination**:
 
 
• This method is used for **carbonate ores** or **hydrated oxides**. It involves heating the ore strongly in the **absence** or **limited supply of air**.
 
• During calcination, **carbon dioxide** or **water vapor** is expelled. For example, **Zinc carbonate (ZnCO3)** is heated to obtain **Zinc oxide (ZnO)**.
 
 
 
• **Reduction with Carbon (Smelting)**:
 
 
• Metals in the **middle of the reactivity series**, such as **Zinc (Zn)**, **Iron (Fe)**, **Tin (Sn)**, and **Lead (Pb)**, are extracted using this method.
 
• Once the ores are converted to oxides via roasting or calcination, they are heated with **carbon (coke)**, which acts as a **reducing agent** to produce the free metal.
 
 
 
• **Reactivity Series Context**:
 
 
• Metals at the **bottom of the series**, like **Gold (Au)** and **Platinum (Pt)**, exist in their **native state** (free form) due to their lack of reactivity.
 
• Metals like **Mercury (Hg)** can be extracted simply by **heating** their sulfide ore, **Cinnabar (HgS)**, in air without needing a separate reducing agent.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cathode Reaction**: In the extraction of **Sodium**, the reaction at the **negative electrode** is **Na+ + e- → Na**.
 
• **Anode Reaction**: At the **positive electrode**, the non-metal (like **Chlorine**) is liberated: **2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e-**.
 
• The **purity** of metals obtained via **electrolytic reduction** is generally very high compared to those obtained by chemical reduction with carbon.
 
• The **reactivity series** is a crucial tool in **metallurgy** for determining the most **economical** and **scientifically valid** method for metal extraction.

questions.question: As the chest cavity becomes larger, air is __________ into the lungs and fills the expanded __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**pulled; alveoli**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The process of breathing, specifically **inhalation** (inspiration), is driven by changes in the volume and pressure of the **chest cavity** (thoracic cavity). When the **diaphragm** and **external intercostal muscles** contract, the **chest cavity** becomes larger.
 
• According to **Boyle's Law**, there is an inverse relationship between the volume and pressure of a gas. As the volume of the **thoracic cavity** increases, the internal **air pressure** within the lungs drops below the **atmospheric pressure**.
 
• Because air naturally flows from an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure, air is **pulled** into the lungs from the external environment. ***Hence, the first part of the statement is "pulled".***
 
• Once the air enters the respiratory system, it passes through the **trachea**, **bronchi**, and **bronchioles**, finally reaching the **alveoli**. These are tiny, balloon-like air sacs that expand to accommodate the incoming air.
 
• The **alveoli** are the primary sites for **gas exchange**. Their walls are extremely thin, allowing **oxygen** to move into the blood and **carbon dioxide** to move out. ***Hence, the second part of the statement is "alveoli".***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mechanism of Inhalation:**
 
 
• During **inspiration**, the **diaphragm** (a dome-shaped muscle) flattens and moves downward. Simultaneously, the **intercostal muscles** pull the **ribs** upward and outward.
 
• This dual action expands the **thoracic volume** in both the vertical and anteroposterior planes, creating the **negative pressure** required to draw air in.
 
 
 
• **Mechanism of Exhalation:**
 
 
• **Exhalation** (expiration) is generally a passive process at rest. The **diaphragm** and **intercostal muscles** relax, causing the **chest cavity** to decrease in size.
 
• The **elastic recoil** of the lung tissue increases the internal pressure, causing air to be **pushed** out of the lungs.
 
 
 
• **Structure of the Alveoli:**
 
 
• The human lungs contain approximately **300 to 500 million alveoli**, providing a massive **surface area** (about **70 to 100 square meters**) for efficient gas exchange.
 
• They are coated with a substance called **surfactant**, which prevents the **alveoli** from collapsing by reducing **surface tension**.
 
 
 
• **Respiratory Anatomy:**
 
 
• **Bronchi**: These are the two large tubes that carry air from the **trachea** into the **lungs**. They branch into smaller **bronchioles**.
 
• **Diaphragm**: The most important muscle of **respiration**, separating the **thoracic cavity** from the **abdominal cavity**.
 
• **Pleura**: A double-layered **serous membrane** that encloses the lungs, ensuring they slide smoothly against the **chest wall** during expansion.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The average adult has a **respiratory rate** of **12 to 16 breaths per minute** at rest.
 
• **Boyle’s Law** application: If volume doubles, pressure is halved. This principle is fundamental to the **mechanical ventilation** of the lungs.
 
• The **partial pressure** of oxygen in the **alveoli** is higher than in the **pulmonary capillaries**, which is why **oxygen** diffuses into the blood.
 
• Conversely, the **partial pressure** of **carbon dioxide** is higher in the blood than in the **alveoli**, facilitating its movement into the **alveoli** to be exhaled.

questions.question: Which two forms of energy are collectively known as mechanical energy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kinetic and Potential energy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mechanical energy** is the sum of **potential energy** and **kinetic energy** present in the components of a mechanical system. It is the energy associated with the **motion** and **position** of an object.
 
• **Kinetic Energy** is the form of energy that an object or a particle has by reason of its **motion**. If work, which transfers energy, is done on an object by applying a net force, the object speeds up and thereby gains kinetic energy.
 
• **Potential Energy** is the stored energy possessed by an object because of its **position** relative to others, stresses within itself, its **electric charge**, or other factors. The most common types are **gravitational potential energy** and **elastic potential energy**.
 
• The relationship is expressed by the formula: **Mechanical Energy (E) = Kinetic Energy (K) + Potential Energy (U)**.
 
• When an object is in motion, it possesses **Kinetic Energy**, and when it is at a certain height or in a deformed state (like a stretched spring), it possesses **Potential Energy**. The combination of these two determines the total mechanical capacity of the object to do work. ***Hence, the correct answer is Kinetic and Potential energy.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kinetic Energy (KE):**
 
 
• The **numerical value** of kinetic energy is calculated using the formula **K = 1/2 mv²**, where **m** is the **mass** of the object and **v** is its **magnitude of velocity** (speed).
 
• Examples include a **moving car**, **flowing water** in a river, or a **flying bird**. Since it depends on the square of velocity, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.
 
 
 
• **Potential Energy (PE):**
 
 
• **Gravitational Potential Energy** is calculated as **U = mgh**, where **m** is **mass**, **g** is the **acceleration due to gravity** (approximately **9.8 m/s²** on Earth), and **h** is the **height** above a reference point.
 
• **Elastic Potential Energy** is stored in objects that can be **compressed** or **stretched**, such as **rubber bands**, **springs**, or a **drawn archer's bow**.
 
 
 
• **Other Forms of Energy mentioned in options:**
 
 
• **Heat Energy:** Also known as **thermal energy**, it arises from the internal motion of atoms and molecules within a substance.
 
• **Chemical Energy:** Energy stored in the **bonds** of chemical compounds, such as in **batteries**, **food**, or **gasoline**.
 
• **Nuclear Energy:** Energy released during **nuclear fission** or **fusion**, originating from the **nucleus** of an atom.
 
• **Electrical Energy:** Energy caused by the **moving electric charges** (electrons).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy:** In an **isolated system** where only **conservative forces** (like gravity) are acting, the total **mechanical energy** remains **constant** over **time**. This means the loss in potential energy is equal to the gain in kinetic energy, and vice versa.
 
• **Unit of Energy:** The **SI unit** for all forms of energy, including mechanical, kinetic, and potential, is the **Joule (J)**. One Joule is defined as the work done by a force of **one Newton** acting through a distance of **one meter**.
 
• **Work-Energy Theorem:** This principle states that the **net work** done by all forces acting on an object is equal to the **change in its kinetic energy**.
 
• **Transformation Example:** In a **hydroelectric power plant**, water stored at a **height** in a dam has high **potential energy**. As the water falls, this potential energy is converted into **kinetic energy**, which then turns **turbines** to produce **electricity**.

questions.question: Which acid does NOT give hydrogen gas when treated with metal because of its oxidising nature?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nitric acid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Nitric acid** (**HNO3**) is a powerful **oxidizing agent**. Unlike other mineral acids, when it reacts with most metals, it does not release **hydrogen gas** (**H2**).
 
• This phenomenon occurs because the **hydrogen gas** produced during the initial reaction is immediately oxidized by the acid into **water** (**H2O**). ***Hence, the statement regarding its oxidizing nature is correct.***
 
• During this process, the **Nitric acid** itself undergoes **reduction** to form various **nitrogen oxides**, such as **nitrogen dioxide** (**NO2**), **nitric oxide** (**NO**), or **nitrous oxide** (**N2O**), depending on the concentration of the acid and the temperature.
 
• However, there are specific exceptions to this rule. When **very dilute nitric acid** (around **1%** concentration) reacts with **Magnesium** (**Mg**) and **Manganese** (**Mn**), **hydrogen gas** is actually evolved.
 
• In contrast, metals like **Copper**, **Silver**, and **Mercury** react with **concentrated nitric acid** to yield **salt**, **water**, and **nitrogen dioxide**, but no **hydrogen gas** is liberated.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hydrochloric Acid (HCl):**
 
 
• It is a **strong acid** and a major component of **gastric acid** in the **human digestive system**.
 
• When **HCl** reacts with active metals such as **Zinc** (**Zn**), **Iron** (**Fe**), or **Aluminium** (**Al**), it readily produces **metal chlorides** and evolves **hydrogen gas**. For example: **Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2**.
 
 
 
• **Sulphuric Acid (H2SO4):**
 
 
• Known as the **'King of Chemicals'**, it is widely used in **lead-acid batteries** and **fertilizer production**.
 
• **Dilute sulphuric acid** reacts with metals positioned above **hydrogen** in the **reactivity series** to liberate **hydrogen gas** and form **metal sulphates**. However, **concentrated sulphuric acid** acts as an **oxidizing agent** and behaves differently, often producing **sulphur dioxide** (**SO2**).
 
 
 
• **Acetic Acid (CH3COOH):**
 
 
• This is a **weak organic acid** and the primary constituent of **vinegar** (typically **5-8%** by volume).
 
• It reacts with metals like **Magnesium** or **Zinc** to form **metal acetates** and slowly releases **hydrogen gas**. Because it is a **weak acid**, the rate of **hydrogen evolution** is much slower compared to **HCl** or **H2SO4**.
 
 
 
• **The Reactivity Series:**
 
 
• The ability of an acid to displace **hydrogen** depends on the position of the metal in the **activity series**.
 
• Metals like **Gold** (**Au**) and **Platinum** (**Pt**) do not react with these individual acids and require **Aqua Regia** (a mixture of **concentrated HCl** and **concentrated HNO3** in a **3:1 ratio**) for dissolution.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Oxidation State:** In **Nitric acid**, **Nitrogen** is in its maximum **oxidation state** of **+5**. This makes the molecule highly unstable and eager to accept **electrons**, facilitating its **strong oxidizing** properties.
 
• **Industrial Use:** **Nitric acid** is vital in the **manufacture of explosives** like **TNT** (**Trinitrotoluene**) and **Nitroglycerin**, as well as in the production of **ammonium nitrate** for **agricultural fertilizers**.
 
• **Safety:** **Nitric acid** is highly **corrosive** and can cause severe **chemical burns**. It turns **human skin yellow** upon contact due to a reaction with **proteins** known as the **xanthoproteic reaction**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about evaporation is true?

options.text: It occurs only at boiling point
It occurs only at the surface of the liquid

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It occurs only at the surface of the liquid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Evaporation** is a type of **vaporization** that occurs on the surface of a liquid as it changes into the gas phase.
 
• It is strictly a **surface phenomenon** because only the molecules at the top layer of the liquid possess enough **kinetic energy** to overcome the **intermolecular forces** of attraction and escape into the atmosphere. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• Contrary to some misconceptions, evaporation **requires heat** energy, known as the **Latent Heat of Vaporization**, which is absorbed from the surroundings or the liquid itself. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• **Evaporation** can take place at **any temperature** below the boiling point of the liquid, whereas **boiling** only occurs at a specific, fixed **boiling point**. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• While **boiling** is a **bulk phenomenon** that occurs throughout the entire volume of the liquid (indicated by the formation of bubbles), evaporation is limited to the surface. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Factors Affecting Evaporation:**
 
 
• **Surface Area**: Since it is a surface phenomenon, an increase in the **surface area** leads to an increase in the **rate of evaporation**. For example, spreading out wet clothes helps them dry faster.
 
• **Temperature**: An increase in **temperature** provides more particles with enough **kinetic energy** to go into the vapor state, thereby increasing the rate.
 
• **Humidity**: This refers to the amount of water vapor present in the air. If **humidity** is high, the air cannot hold much more moisture, so the rate of evaporation decreases.
 
• **Wind Speed**: With an increase in **wind speed**, water vapor particles move away with the wind, decreasing the amount of water vapor in the surrounding area and increasing evaporation.
 
 
 
• **Cooling Effect:**
 
 
• One of the most important features of evaporation is that it causes **cooling**. As the liquid evaporates, it draws energy (heat) from the surface it is in contact with, resulting in a temperature drop.
 
• **Examples**: Human **sweating** helps regulate body temperature, and water kept in **earthen pots** (matkas) stays cool due to evaporation through porous walls.
 
 
 
• **Molecular Mechanism:**
 
 
• In a liquid, molecules are in constant motion with varying speeds. Only those at the **surface** with high **velocity** can break free from the cohesive forces of the liquid bulk. This explains why the remaining liquid becomes cooler, as the "hottest" (highest energy) molecules are the ones that leave first.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Difference between Evaporation and Boiling:**
 
 
• **Evaporation** is a **slow process**, while **boiling** is a **fast process**.
 
• **Evaporation** occurs at the **surface**, whereas **boiling** occurs throughout the **entire mass** of the liquid.
 
• **Evaporation** leads to **cooling**, but **boiling** does not produce a cooling effect on the substance itself while it is being heated.
 
• **Boiling** happens only when the **vapor pressure** of the liquid equals the **atmospheric pressure**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Match the following body parts with the types of epithelial tissue found in them.
 
 **Body parts** **Epithelial tissue** 
 A. Kidney tubules 1. Stratified squamous epithelial 
 B. Surface of skin 2. Cuboidal epithelium 
 C. Lung alveoli 3. Ciliated columnar epithelium 
 D. Respiratory tract lining 4. Simple squamous epithelium
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A - 2, B - 1, C - 4, D - 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kidney Tubules (Cuboidal Epithelium)**:
 
 
• The **cuboidal epithelium** consists of **cube-like cells** that are roughly as tall as they are wide.
 
• In the **kidney tubules** (specifically the proximal convoluted tubule), these cells often possess **microvilli** to facilitate **secretion and absorption**. ***Hence, A matches with 2 is correct.***
 
 
 
• **Surface of Skin (Stratified Squamous Epithelial)**:
 
 
• The **skin** is subjected to constant **wear and tear**; therefore, it is composed of **stratified squamous epithelium**, which consists of **multiple layers** of cells.
 
• The **outermost layer** of the skin is **keratinized** to provide a **waterproof** and **protective barrier** against mechanical injury and pathogens. ***Hence, B matches with 1 is correct.***
 
 
 
• **Lung Alveoli (Simple Squamous Epithelium)**:
 
 
• **Simple squamous epithelium** is a **single layer** of extremely **thin and flat cells**, forming a delicate lining.
 
• This tissue is found in the **lung alveoli** and **blood vessels**, where the **transport of substances** or **gas exchange** occurs through a **selectively permeable surface**. ***Hence, C matches with 4 is correct.***
 
 
 
• **Respiratory Tract Lining (Ciliated Columnar Epithelium)**:
 
 
• In the **respiratory tract**, the **columnar epithelial** cells possess hair-like projections called **cilia** on their outer surfaces.
 
• These **cilia** can move, and their rhythmic motion pushes **mucus** forward to clear the tract. ***Hence, D matches with 3 is correct.***
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Classification of Epithelial Tissues**:
 
 
• **Epithelial tissues** are classified based on the **number of cell layers** and the **shape of the cells**.
 
• **Simple epithelium** consists of a **single layer** of cells, typically found where **absorption, secretion, or filtration** occurs.
 
• **Stratified epithelium** consists of **two or more layers** of cells, primarily serving a **protective function** in areas prone to **friction**.
 
 
 
• **Specialized Functions**:
 
 
• **Glandular Epithelium**: Sometimes a portion of the epithelial tissue folds inward, forming **multicellular glands** responsible for **secreting substances** like sweat, oil, or digestive enzymes.
 
• **Columnar Epithelium**: Characterized by tall, **pillar-like cells**, it is found in the **inner lining of the intestine** where **absorption and secretion** are prominent.
 
 
 
• **Structural Integrity**:
 
 
• All epithelial cells are usually separated from the underlying tissue by an **extracellular fibrous basement membrane**.
 
• There is **very little intercellular space** between the cells, making them a **continuous sheet** that acts as a **barrier** to keep different body systems separate.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Simple Squamous**: Located in **Bowman's capsule** and **capillaries**; functions include **filtration**.
 
• **Simple Cuboidal**: Located in **thyroid vesicles** and **salivary gland ducts**; functions include **mechanical support**.
 
• **Stratified Squamous**: Non-keratinized type is found in the **esophagus** and **lining of the mouth**.
 
• **Ciliated Columnar**: Also found in the **fallopian tubes** (oviducts) to help move the **ovum** toward the uterus.
</ul

questions.question: Who first observed the densely stained reticular structures near the nucleus, now known as Golgi bodies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Camillo Golgi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Camillo Golgi**, an **Italian** physician and pathologist, first observed the **densely stained reticular structures** near the **nucleus** of a cell in the year **1898**.
 
• He discovered these structures while investigating the **nervous system** using a unique staining technique he developed, known as the **"black reaction"** (la reazione nera), which utilized **silver nitrate**.
 
• These reticular networks were later named **Golgi bodies** (also known as the **Golgi apparatus** or **Golgi complex**) in his honor.
 
• The **Golgi apparatus** is a membrane-bound organelle found in most **eukaryotic cells** and is characterized by a series of flattened, stacked pouches called **cisternae**.
 
• For his revolutionary work on the structure of the **nervous system**, **Camillo Golgi** was awarded the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** in **1906**, sharing it with **Santiago Ramón y Cajal**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Robert Hooke**:
 
 
• In **1665**, **Robert Hooke** observed thin slices of **cork** under a primitive **compound microscope**.
 
• He observed **honeycomb-like** structures and coined the term **"cell"** to describe them, although he was actually looking at the **dead cell walls** of plant tissue.
 
 
 
• **Anton van Leeuwenhoek**:
 
 
• Commonly known as the **"Father of Microbiology,"** **Leeuwenhoek** was a **Dutch** scientist who, in **1674**, was the first to observe and describe **live cells**.
 
• Using his high-quality **single-lens microscopes**, he discovered **bacteria**, **protozoa** (which he called "animalcules"), and **human sperm cells**.
 
 
 
• **Matthias Schleiden**:
 
 
• In **1838**, **Matthias Schleiden**, a **German botanist**, concluded that all **plant tissues** are composed of cells.
 
• His work, along with that of **Theodor Schwann**, formed the basis of the **Cell Theory**, which states that the **cell** is the basic unit of life.
 
 
 
• **Functions and Features of Golgi Bodies**:
 
 
• The primary function of the **Golgi apparatus** is the **packaging**, **modification**, and **sorting** of proteins and lipids that are synthesized in the **Endoplasmic Reticulum**.
 
• It acts like a **"post office"** of the cell, tagging molecules with **carbohydrates** or **phosphates** to ensure they reach their correct destination, such as the **cell membrane** or **lysosomes**.
 
• It has a distinct polarity, with a **cis face** (receiving side near the ER) and a **trans face** (shipping side).

questions.question: Which of the following is a displacement reaction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **displacement reaction** is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. These reactions are also known as **substitution reactions** or **single displacement reactions**.
 
• In the reaction **Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu**, **Zinc (Zn)** is a more reactive metal than **Copper (Cu)**. When **Zinc** is added to a **blue** solution of **Copper (II) sulphate**, it displaces the **Copper** atoms to form **Zinc sulphate** and solid **Copper**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• The reaction **CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2** represents a **decomposition reaction**. In this process, a single reactant (**Calcium Carbonate**) breaks down into two or more simpler products (**Calcium Oxide** and **Carbon Dioxide**) upon the application of **heat**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The reaction **AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3** is an example of a **double displacement reaction** (specifically a **precipitation reaction**). Here, two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds, resulting in the formation of an insoluble white precipitate of **Silver Chloride (AgCl)**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The reaction **NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O** is a **neutralization reaction**. It occurs between a **base (Sodium Hydroxide)** and an **acid (Hydrochloric Acid)** to produce **salt (Sodium Chloride)** and **water**. This is also categorized as a type of **double displacement**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Reactivity Series of Metals:**
 
 
• The ability of one metal to displace another is determined by the **reactivity series**. This is a list of metals arranged in decreasing order of their **reactivity**.
 
• Metals like **Potassium (K)**, **Sodium (Na)**, and **Calcium (Ca)** are at the top and are highly reactive.
 
• **Zinc (Zn)** is placed higher than **Copper (Cu)**, **Silver (Ag)**, and **Gold (Au)** in the series, which explains why **Zinc** can displace **Copper** from its salt solution.
 
 
 
• **Observation in Displacement Reactions:**
 
 
• In the **Zn + CuSO4** reaction, the characteristic **blue color** of the **CuSO4** solution fades and eventually becomes **colorless** as **ZnSO4** is formed.
 
• A **reddish-brown** deposit of **Copper** metal can be seen on the **Zinc** strip or at the bottom of the beaker.
 
 
 
• **Types of Displacement:**
 
 
• **Single Displacement:** One element replaces another in a compound (e.g., **Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu**).
 
• **Double Displacement:** Two compounds exchange their **cations** and **anions** to form new products (e.g., **BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl**).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Reactivity Order:** The general order of reactivity for common metals is **K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au**.
 
• **Non-Metal Displacement:** Displacement reactions are not limited to metals. For example, a more reactive **halogen** can displace a less reactive **halogen** from its halide (e.g., **Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2**).
 
• **Applications:** These reactions are widely used in **metallurgy** for the extraction of metals, in **thermite welding** (where **Aluminum** displaces **Iron** from its oxide), and in **electrochemical cells**.
 
• **Law of Conservation of Mass:** Every chemical equation must be **balanced** to satisfy this law, ensuring the **number** of atoms of each element remains the same before and after the reaction.
</ul

questions.question: The slope of a distance-time graph represents the:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**speed of the object**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **distance-time graph** is a graphical representation used to show how the **distance** traveled by an object changes over a specific **period of time**.
 
• In this graph, **distance** is typically plotted on the **vertical axis (y-axis)**, and **time** is plotted on the **horizontal axis (x-axis)**.
 
• The **slope** (also known as the **gradient**) of a line on any graph is calculated as the **vertical change** divided by the **horizontal change** (Rise/Run).
 
• For a distance-time graph, the **slope** is equal to the **change in distance** divided by the **change in time**. Mathematically, this is the formula for **speed** (**Speed = Distance / Time**). ***Hence, the correct answer is speed of the object.***
 
• If the **slope** is a **straight line** passing through the origin, it indicates that the object is moving at a **constant speed**.
 
• A **steeper slope** represents a **higher speed**, whereas a **gentler slope** represents a **lower speed**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Acceleration of the object:**
 
 
• **Acceleration** is the rate of **change of velocity** per unit of **time**.
 
• It is represented by the **slope** of a **velocity-time graph**, not a distance-time graph.
 
• If a distance-time graph is a **curve** (such as a parabola), it indicates that the **speed** is changing, which implies the object is undergoing **acceleration**.
 
 
 
• **Force on the object:**
 
 
• According to **Newton's Second Law of Motion**, **Force (F)** is equal to the product of **mass (m)** and **acceleration (a)**.
 
• While **force** influences the motion depicted on a graph, it is not directly read from the **slope** of a simple distance-time graph without knowing the **mass**.
 
 
 
• **Distance covered:**
 
 
• The **total distance covered** by an object at any specific **time** is represented by the **magnitude** of the **y-coordinate** at that point on the graph.
 
• It is a **scalar quantity** that refers to "how much ground an object has covered" during its motion.
 
 
 
• **Types of Motion on Distance-Time Graphs:**
 
 
• **Stationary Object:** Represented by a **horizontal line** where the **slope is zero**.
 
• **Uniform Motion:** Represented by a **straight slanted line** indicating **constant speed**.
 
• **Non-Uniform Motion:** Represented by a **curved line**, showing that the **speed** is either increasing or decreasing.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Standard International (SI) unit** of **speed** is **meters per second (m/s)**.
 
• The **slope** of a **displacement-time graph** represents the **velocity** of the object, which is a **vector quantity** (includes direction).
 
• The **area** under a **velocity-time graph** represents the total **displacement** or **distance** traveled by the object during a **time interval**.
 
• In **kinematics**, these graphs are essential for visualizing the **equations of motion** developed by **Sir Isaac Newton**.
</ul

questions.question: If an object’s velocity changes uniformly over a period of time, how can the average velocity during that time be calculated?

options.text: By dividing the final velocity by the initial velocity
By adding the initial velocity to twice the final velocity
By subtracting the initial velocity from the final velocity
By taking the arithmetic mean of the initial and final velocities

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By taking the arithmetic mean of the initial and final velocities**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When an object's **velocity** changes at a **constant rate**, it is said to be in **uniform acceleration**. In such cases, the **average velocity** for a specific time interval is calculated as the **arithmetic mean** of its **initial velocity** and **final velocity**.
 
• The mathematical expression for this calculation is **Average Velocity = (u + v) / 2**, where **u** represents the **initial velocity** at the start of the time period and **v** represents the **final velocity** at the end of that period.
 
• This specific formula is only applicable when the **acceleration** is **uniform** (constant). If the acceleration varies over time, the average velocity must be calculated using the **total displacement** divided by the **total time taken**.
 
• The **arithmetic mean** effectively balances the velocity over the duration, providing a representative value of the motion throughout the **period of time**.
 
• Dividing the final velocity by the initial velocity or subtracting them (which gives the change in velocity) does not provide the average state of motion. ***Hence, taking the arithmetic mean is the correct method.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Velocity and its nature:**
 
 
• **Velocity** is a **vector quantity**, meaning it possesses both **magnitude** and **direction**. This distinguishes it from speed, which is a scalar quantity.
 
• The **SI unit** for measuring velocity is **meters per second (m/s)**. Other commonly used units include **kilometers per hour (km/h)**.
 
 
 
• **Uniform Acceleration:**
 
 
• An object is under **uniform acceleration** if its velocity changes by **equal amounts** in **equal intervals of time**.
 
• A common example of **uniform acceleration** is the motion of a freely falling body under **gravity**, where the acceleration is approximately **9.8 m/s²** on Earth.
 
 
 
• **Equations of Motion:**
 
 
• For objects moving with **uniform acceleration** in a straight line, three fundamental equations relate **velocity**, **time**, **displacement**, and **acceleration**.
 
• The first equation is **v = u + at**, the second is **s = ut + ½at²**, and the third is **v² = u² + 2as**. These were formulated by **Isaac Newton**.
 
 
 
• **Average Speed vs. Average Velocity:**
 
 
• **Average Speed** is the **total distance** traveled divided by the **total time** taken. It does not account for direction.
 
• **Average Velocity** is defined as the **total displacement** (the shortest path between initial and final positions) divided by the **total time**. If an object returns to its starting point, its average velocity is **zero**, regardless of the distance covered.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key distinctions in motion:**
 
 
• In **Uniform Motion**, the velocity remains **constant** over time, meaning the **acceleration** is **zero**. In this case, the average velocity is simply the constant velocity itself.
 
• In **Non-Uniform Motion**, the velocity changes at a **non-constant rate**. The simple arithmetic mean formula **(u+v)/2** cannot be used here; instead, **calculus** or the **total displacement/total time** method is required.
 
• The term **Instantaneous Velocity** refers to the velocity of an object at a specific **point in time**, which can be found by taking the derivative of the position with respect to time.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct reason for constructing the ceilings of large halls in a curved shape?

options.text: To allow sound to distribute evenly in the hall
To provide more storage space above the ceiling
To reduce the overall height of the hall

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To allow sound to distribute evenly in the hall**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The ceilings of large **concert halls**, **cinema halls**, and **conference rooms** are made curved so that **sound waves**, after reflecting from the ceiling, reach all corners of the hall.
 
• A curved ceiling (specifically a **concave surface**) acts as a large **sound reflector**. When sound waves hit the curved surface, they are reflected back in a way that distributes the energy **uniformly** across the seating area. ***Hence, the reason is to allow sound to distribute evenly.***
 
• The primary physics principle involved is the **reflection of sound**. Just like light, sound follows the law where the **angle of incidence** is equal to the **angle of reflection**.
 
• Without a curved ceiling, sound might only reach the front rows clearly, while the back rows might experience "dead zones" or very faint sound levels.
 
• The design ensures that the **intensity** of the sound remains consistent for every audience member, regardless of their **location** in the hall.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reverberation:**
 
 
• In a large hall, sound can persist due to repeated reflections from the walls, ceiling, and floor. This persistence of sound is known as **reverberation**.
 
• If the **reverberation time** is too long, the sound becomes blurred and distorted. To control this, architects use **sound-absorbent materials** like **compressed fiberboard**, **rough plaster**, or **heavy curtains** on the walls.
 
 
 
• **Soundboards:**
 
 
• In some auditoriums, a **curved soundboard** is placed behind the speaker or the stage. The speaker is positioned at the **focus** of this concave board so that sound waves are reflected as **parallel beams** toward the audience.
 
 
 
• **Echo vs. Reflection:**
 
 
• An **echo** is a distinct reflected sound heard after a specific interval. To hear a clear echo, the minimum distance between the source and the reflecting surface must be approximately **17.2 meters** (assuming the speed of sound is **344 m/s** at **22 degrees Celsius**).
 
• The **sensation of sound** persists in the human brain for about **0.1 seconds**.
 
 
 
• **Multiple Reflection Applications:**
 
 
• **Stethoscopes**: Use the principle of **multiple reflection** of sound to transport the sound of the patient’s heartbeat to the doctor's ears through a tube.
 
• **Megaphones and Horns**: These are designed to send sound in a particular direction by using multiple reflections within a **conical** opening, preventing the sound from spreading in all directions.
 
 
 
• **Acoustic Design Materials:**
 
 
• Apart from structural shapes, materials like **perforated cardboard** and **soft carpets** are used to manage **acoustic properties** and reduce unwanted noise in professional environments.

Falling of an apple from a tree

__
 
• The **Universal Law of Gravitation**, formulated by **Sir Isaac Newton** in **1687**, states that every particle of matter in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their **masses** and inversely proportional to the square of the **distance** between them.
 
• **Tides in the ocean** are primarily caused by the **gravitational pull** of the **Moon** and the **Sun** acting on the **Earth's** water bodies. As the **Earth** rotates, this pull creates the periodic rise and fall of sea levels. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct (it is explained by gravitation).***
 
• **Attraction between magnets** is a phenomenon governed by the **electromagnetic force**, specifically **magnetic fields** generated by moving **electric charges** or **intrinsic magnetic moments** of electrons. While magnets have **mass** and exert a negligible gravitational pull on each other, the force that causes them to snap together is not **gravity**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect (it cannot be explained by gravitation).***
 
• The **revolution of the Moon around the Earth** is maintained by the **gravitational force** of the **Earth**, which provides the necessary **centripetal force** to keep the **Moon** in its nearly circular **orbit**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct (it is explained by gravitation).***
 
• The **falling of an apple from a tree** toward the ground is the classic example used to describe **Earth's gravity**. The **Earth** exerts an attractive force on the **mass** of the apple, causing it to accelerate at approximately **9.8 m/s²**. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct (it is explained by gravitation).***
 
• The mathematical expression for this law is **F = G(m1m2/r²)**, where **G** is the **Universal Gravitational Constant**.

__
 
• **Fundamental Forces of Nature:**
 
 
• There are **four fundamental forces**: **Gravitational Force**, **Electromagnetic Force**, **Strong Nuclear Force**, and **Weak Nuclear Force**.
 
• **Gravitational Force** is the weakest of the four but has an **infinite range** and is always **attractive**.
 
• **Electromagnetic Force** acts between **charged particles** and can be either **attractive or repulsive**. It is significantly stronger than **gravity** at small scales.
 
 
 
• **Newton's Principia Mathematica:**
 
 
• **Newton** published his findings in the **Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica** in **July 1687**, which laid the foundations for **classical mechanics**.
 
• The law explains not only terrestrial motion but also the **motion of planets** in the **solar system**, verifying **Kepler's laws of planetary motion**.
 
 
 
• **Universal Gravitational Constant (G):**
 
 
• The value of **G** was first accurately measured by **Henry Cavendish** in **1798** using a **torsion balance**.
 
• The modern accepted value is approximately **6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N⋅m²/kg²**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Inverse Square Law:**
 
 
• Because the force is **inversely proportional** to the **square of the distance**, doubling the distance between two objects reduces the **gravitational pull** to **one-fourth** of its original strength.
 
 
 
• **Centripetal Force in Orbits:**
 
 
• In the case of **satellites** or **planets**, the **gravitational force** acts as the **centripetal force**, which is required for **curved motion**. Without this force, objects would move in a **straight line** due to **inertia**.

We know the direct algebraic identity: (a + b)² − (a − b)² = 4ab

questions.question: As of May 2025, what is the maximum FDI allowed through the Automatic Route in India's defense sector for companies seeking new industrial licenses?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**74%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• As of **May 2025**, the Government of India permits Foreign Direct Investment (**FDI**) in the defense sector up to **74%** through the **Automatic Route** for companies seeking new industrial licenses.
 
• This significant policy shift was formalized through **Press Note 4 (2020 Series)** issued by the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)** in **September 2020**, aimed at boosting local manufacturing.
 
• For investments exceeding **74%**, the **Government Route** is applicable, allowing up to **100%** FDI where it is likely to result in access to modern technology or for other reasons to be recorded by the government.
 
• The policy stipulates that any foreign investment in the defense sector is subject to **Security Clearance** by the **Ministry of Home Affairs** and as per the guidelines of the **Ministry of Defence**.
 
• The liberalization of FDI limits is a core component of the **Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan** (Self-Reliant India Mission), designed to encourage **Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs)** to set up production facilities within **India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Evolution of FDI in Defense:**
 
 
• In **2001**, the defense sector was first opened to private participation with an FDI cap of **26%**.
 
• The limit was increased to **49%** under the **Automatic Route** in **2014** to stimulate the **Make in India** initiative.
 
• The current **74%** limit serves to provide foreign investors with management control, thereby incentivizing the transfer of high-end technology to **Indian** subsidiaries.
 
 
 
• **Automatic vs. Government Route:**
 
 
• The **Automatic Route** signifies that the foreign investor or the Indian company does not require any prior approval from the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** or the **Government of India** for the investment.
 
• The **Government Route** (or Approval Route) requires prior clearance from the concerned administrative ministry, which in this case is the **Ministry of Defence**.
 
 
 
• **Regulatory Framework:**
 
 
• Defense manufacturing is primarily regulated under the **Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951** and the **Arms Act, 1959**.
 
• All foreign investments are subject to **National Security** clauses, allowing the government to review any investment that may affect the sovereignty and integrity of the nation.
 
 
 
• **Sectoral Impact:**
 
 
• The increase to **74%** has facilitated major global firms like **Safran**, **Lockheed Martin**, and **Boeing** to explore deeper collaborations with **Indian** partners.
 
• It aims to reduce the **Defense Import Bill**, as **India** has historically been one of the world's largest importers of major arms.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fresh Industrial Licenses:** The **74%** automatic limit is specifically applicable to companies seeking **New Industrial Licenses**. Existing licensees seeking to infuse fresh foreign investment up to **49%** must follow specific declaration protocols.
 
• **Review Authority:** The **Department of Defence Production (DDP)** functions as the nodal agency for processing cases under the **Government Route** and monitors the **Indigenization** progress.
 
• **Equity Cap:** While the **74%** route is automatic, the government maintains the right to scrutinize any investment on the grounds of **Security**, ensuring that the control of critical defense infrastructure remains transparent.
</ul

questions.question: ‘Agnibaan - SOrTeD’ (Sub-Orbital Technology Demonstrator) was launched on 30 May 2024 from India's first private launch pad called ______, established by Agnikul.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dhanush**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Agnibaan - SOrTeD** (**Sub-Orbital Technological Demonstrator**) mission was successfully launched on **30 May 2024**.
 
• It was launched from **Dhanush**, which is **India's first private launchpad**, established by the space startup **Agnikul Cosmos**.
 
• The **Dhanush** launchpad is located within the premises of the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** (**SDSC SHAR**) in **Sriharikota**, **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• This mission marked a significant milestone as it was the **first-ever launch** from a private launchpad in **India** and featured the world's first **single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine**, named **Agnilet**.
 
• The flight was a **sub-orbital mission**, designed to test the flight systems and the **3D-printed engine** technology before full-scale orbital launches.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Agnikul Cosmos**:
 
 
• It is an **IIT Madras**-incubated space startup founded in **2017** by **Srinath Ravichandran** and **Moin SPM**.
 
• The company focuses on developing **cost-effective** and **customizable** launch vehicles for small satellites.
 
• In **2022**, **Agnikul** inaugurated **India's first private launchpad** and mission control center at **Sriharikota**.
 
 
 
• **Agnilet Engine**:
 
 
• The **Agnilet** is a **semi-cryogenic engine** that uses **Liquid Oxygen** (**LOX**) and **Kerosene** as propellants.
 
• It is unique because it is **entirely 3D-printed** as a **single piece** of hardware, significantly reducing the number of components and assembly time.
 
 
 
• **Regulatory Framework**:
 
 
• The launch was supported by **IN-SPACe** (**Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre**) and **ISRO** (**Indian Space Research Organisation**).
 
• **IN-SPACe** acts as a single-window nodal agency to promote and authorize **private sector participation** in the **Indian space sector**.
 
 
 
• **Significance for the Indian Space Sector**:
 
 
• Following the success of **Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-S** in **November 2022**, the **Agnibaan** mission further cements **India’s** position in the global **private space industry**.
 
• The use of **additive manufacturing** (**3D printing**) in rocket engines showcases **India's** technological advancements in **deep-tech** sectors.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Agnibaan** rocket is a **customizable**, **two-stage** launch vehicle capable of carrying a payload of up to **100 kg** to a **Low Earth Orbit** (**LEO**) of about **700 km**.
 
• The **SOrTeD** mission specifically utilized a **single-stage** version of the rocket to demonstrate **vertical ascent** and **controlled flight**.
 
• The establishment of **private launchpads** like **Dhanush** is part of the **Indian Space Policy 2023**, which encourages **Non-Government Entities** (**NGEs**) to own and operate space infrastructure.

• The survey attributes this optimistic growth projection to the expectation of a **normal monsoon** and favorable **reservoir levels** across the country, which are critical for the **Kharif** and **Rabi** sowing seasons.
 
• The agriculture sector remains a vital pillar of the Indian economy, contributing approximately **18-19%** to the **Gross Value Added (GVA)** and providing a livelihood for nearly **45%** of the population.
 
• The improvement in agricultural output is expected to boost **rural demand**, which in turn supports the broader recovery of the **Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG)** and **automobile** sectors.

• **Role of the Economic Survey**: 
 
 
• The **Economic Survey** is a flagship document prepared by the **Department of Economic Affairs** under the **Ministry of Finance**.
 
• It is authored by the **Chief Economic Advisor (CEA)** of India, a position currently held by **Dr. V. Anantha Nageswaran**.
 
• The document provides a detailed report card of the economy for the closing financial year and offers insights and outlooks for the upcoming year.
 
 
 
• **Focus on Food Inflation**:

__
 
• **Manoj Kumar** is a legendary **Indian** actor, director, and screenwriter who became an iconic figure in **Bollywood** during the **1960s** and **1970s**.
 
• He earned the popular moniker "**Bharat Kumar**" due to his penchant for acting in and directing films with strong **patriotic** themes, where his character was often named **Bharat**.
 
• The veteran actor-director passed away on **4 April 2025** (as per the provided data), marking the end of a cinematic era dedicated to **nationalism** and **Indian** values.
 
• His significant contribution to cinema was recognized by the **Government of India** with the **Dadasaheb Phalke Award** in **2015**, which is the highest honor in **Indian** cinema.
 
• He is best remembered for his "patriotic trilogy" of films: **Shaheed** (**1965**), **Upkar** (**1967**), and **Purab Aur Paschim** (**1970**).
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Manoj Kumar.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Early Life and Background**:
 
 
• Born as **Harikishan Giri Goswami** on **July 24, 1937**, in **Abbottabad** (then part of **British India**, now in **Pakistan**).
 
• His family migrated to **Delhi** during the **Partition of India** in **1947**.
 
• He adopted the screen name **Manoj Kumar** after being inspired by **Dilip Kumar's** character in the **1949** film **Shabnam**.
 
 
 
• **Directorial Milestones**:
 
 
• His directorial debut, **Upkar** (**1967**), was produced at the request of Prime Minister **Lal Bahadur Shastri** to promote the slogan "**Jai Jawan Jai Kisan**" following the **Indo-Pakistani War of 1965**.
 
• In **1974**, he directed **Roti Kapada Aur Makaan**, a massive hit that addressed social issues like unemployment and poverty in **India**.
 
• His **1981** film **Kranti** was another major success that focused on the **Indian Independence Movement**.
 
 
 
• **Awards and Honors**:
 
 
• He received the **Padma Shri**, India's fourth-highest civilian award, in the year **1992**.
 
• Over his career, he won multiple **Filmfare Awards**, including **Best Actor** for **Be-Imaan** (**1972**) and **Best Director** for **Upkar**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Analysis of Other Options**:
 
 
• **Amitabh Bachchan**: Known as the "**Angry Young Man**" and "**Shahenshah**," he was born in **1942** and remains active in the film industry. While he has played patriotic roles, he is not referred to as "**Bharat Kumar**."
 
• **Dilip Kumar**: Often called the "**Tragedy King**," he was one of the greatest actors in **Indian** history. He passed away on **July 7, 2021**, at the **age** of **98**.
 
• **Rajesh Khanna**: Recognized as the first "**Superstar**" of **Indian** cinema, he was famous for his romantic roles and massive fan following in the late **1960s** and early **1970s**. He passed away on **July 18, 2012**.
 
 
 
• **Cinematic Style**:
 
 
• **Manoj Kumar's** films were unique for blending **entertainment** with **socio-political** messages, often contrasting **Western** materialism with **Indian** spiritualism and culture.
 
• His portrayal of **Bhagat Singh** in **Shaheed** remains one of the most authentic depictions of the freedom fighter in **Indian** film **history**.
 
 
</ul
